string-array.name: knowledge_bodies
string-array.item:
Quick glossary:
• Inventory = the beads you have on hand (which colors, how many)
• Bead list = a chart's color-by-color shopping list (how many of each)
• My palette = auto-built from your inventory, using only colors you own

The full beading flow:
① Chart: tap Start a new pattern and pick a photo — the chart is generated automatically; adjust size (29–116), palette and style, then export PDF/PNG.
② Bead-along: in the chart tab turn on Bead-along mode — only the current color lights up. Tap a cell to mark it placed (a ✓ pops up), tap again to undo, hold and drag to sweep a whole run; By board / By row light one board or row at a time and auto-advance when full.
③ Focus: the Focus chip goes fullscreen — prop the phone beside the board and look down; 🔊 Voice speaks progress so your hands stay on the beads.
④ Align: the camera pins the chart onto your real board with 4-point alignment — place beads along the ghost overlay.
⑤ Photo check: photograph your (half-)finished board — it flags likely-wrong/missing/extra beads before you iron.
⑥ Inventory & shopping: log the beads you own, the list suggests substitutes for short colors, and the merged shopping list exports to CSV.
⑦ Archive: finished works live in My projects and reopen anytime; the calendar tracks your beading days.
The ? button on the Bead-along card opens the detailed guide anytime.

Fuse beads (Perler/Hama beads) are plastic tubes about 5mm across with a hole in the middle. Place beads on a pegboard following a chart, cover with ironing paper, and fuse them with a household iron. Once cooled you get a pixel-art piece — keychains, coasters, ornaments, frames and more.

• Standard beads (5mm): the most common kind, most colors, cheap. Each cell is ~0.5cm; one 29×29 board makes about a 15×15cm piece.\n• Mini beads (2.6mm): finer detail for small designs, about half the finished size; harder on the eyes — tweezers recommended.\nNote: the two sizes have different peg spacing and can\'t be mixed on the same board.

Square boards are the most common; a standard 5mm board has 29×29 pegs. Boards snap together for bigger works: 58×58 needs 4, 87×87 needs 9, 116×116 needs 16. Mini beads (2.6mm) commonly use 50×50-peg boards; four snap together into 100×100. Round, hexagon and heart boards are great for small ornaments. For big projects, fasten boards together with linking clips before placing beads.

Common sets come in 24/44/48/60/90/120 colors. More colors = closer photo reproduction: 24 for simple cartoons and emoji, 48–60 for general subjects, 90+ for portraits and scenery.\nBrands: Perler (US), Hama (Denmark), Artkal, plus domestic brands — each has its own code system. Colors in this app are curated approximations; compare with your real beads.\nTip: black, dark blue, dark brown, white and skin tones are usually used the most — stock up.

① When finished, lay ironing paper (or baking paper) over the beads — never touch beads with the iron directly.
② Set the iron to medium (about 120–150°C), steam OFF. Press gently with one hand and move steadily, about 10–20 seconds per side.
③ Peek through the paper: holes slightly shrunk and surface lightly fused is enough; overheating warps the piece.
④ Let it cool completely before peeling the paper; pressing with a heavy book while cooling keeps it flat.
⑤ Flip and repeat. Fusing both sides makes it stronger; add paper and re-iron if edges lift.

• Start from one corner and work row by row, checking each finished row — fewer mistakes.
• Place the few dark outline beads first, then fill large light areas.
• Sort beads into a compartment box and pick them by chart symbol.
• Tweezers save effort and are basically required for mini beads.
• Wrong bead? Don't yank it out — push it out from the back with another bead.

• Photo choice: clear subject + simple background works best (cartoon avatars, pet close-ups, ID photos). For busy portraits, remove the background first or go 87+.
• Size: 29×29 for emoji/chibi, 58×58 for avatars, 87×87+ for half-body and scenery.
• Palette: start with the default 90 colors; if you're missing some, switch to a smaller palette or substitute similar colors while beading.
• Adjustments: pixelation looks a bit "gray" — add saturation (+10~+30) and contrast (+5~+20) to get closer to the original.
• Dithering: smoother gradients but busier charts; beginners should keep it off.

① 3D bead works are just flat panels fused edge to edge.
② Start with a storage box: export five 29×29 charts (a bottom + four walls); for taller walls keep that many solid rows and leave the rest empty.
③ Fusing: iron each panel flat and let it cool, stand them up, align the edges, then run the iron along the seam for 3–5 seconds so the beads fuse; paper clips hold corners while you work.
④ Next steps: pen holder (walls 10–15 rows tall), lamp shade (translucent beads in a cylinder around an LED candle — never a real flame), photo-frame trim.
⑤ Bead counts: chart each face in the app, then let the merged shopping list total everything — buy exactly what you need.

① Keychains: stay within 29×29 (chibi art or a single letter); leave the top row unfused and thread the ring straight through the beads for a stronger hold.
② Fridge magnets: 15×15 to 29×29 mini charts; hot-glue a magnet strip on the back.
③ Coasters: the 29×29 round board is a classic — iron slightly longer for water resistance; gradient sets of four are always popular.
④ Hair clips / brooches: 9×9 to 15×15 mini charts, glued onto clip or pin backs.
⑤ Phone charms / bag tags: use beads with a dedicated side hole, or thread the cord through the top bead row.
⑥ Tip: for gifts, add a date or initials in a corner with the text generator — one tap and it's charted.

How it works: this app runs fully offline — nothing is uploaded. Turning a real photo into an anime face that still looks like you is beyond a low-bead-count medium (it comes out creepy). But you can let any AI assistant convert the photo first, then quantize it into a pattern here — the difference is huge.

Four steps:
① Pick a photo: front-facing or half-body, even lighting, simple background.
② Copy one of the prompts below (tap a button at the bottom of this card), open any AI assistant with image generation/editing (Doubao, Jimeng, Qwen, ChatGPT, Gemini…), upload the photo and paste the prompt.
③ Save the result: prefer a watermark-free export; if there is a watermark, use "Remove watermark" in this app first.
④ Back in the app: Start a new pattern with this image — 58×58 or larger, realistic mode.

Tips:
• Prompt words like "flat color blocks, clean outlines, minimal gradients" are tuned for bead charts — the flatter the AI image, the more it looks like an official pattern after quantization.
• Some platforms restrict real-face photos; try another platform or another photo.
• Every generation is different — save the good one right away.
